prime.problem: "Use every ticket exactly once" sounds like a search over orderings, and greedy walking can strand tickets at a dead end. Backtracking fixes that but can take exponential time. There is a linear answer, and a degree test that tells you in advance whether any answer exists.
prime.fits: Eighth and last graph-basics card. It reuses DFS's explicit stack from the flood-fill card, but writes nodes down when they get stuck (post-order) instead of when they are reached.
expect: dead ends as the end node
prime.goal: Check whether an Eulerian path exists from degrees alone, find it in O(E) after sorting, and explain why writing dead ends first and reversing works.

attend: Why can the start node have one extra out-edge and the end node one extra in-edge, but no other node any imbalance?
When the walk gets stuck, why must the stuck node be the end of the finished path?
Why is the route written last-first and reversed, instead of in walking order?
Why is "every edge once" linear while "every node once" is NP-complete?

must: Every visit to a middle node uses one edge in and one out → balanced degrees everywhere except start (+1 out) and end (+1 in) → the degree test decides existence in O(V + E), plus one connected piece

Walk unused edges until stuck → with balanced degrees the only place you can get stuck first is the end node (or the start, for a circuit) → write it down as last → back up and keep walking → detours found later splice in before it
Hierholzer never undoes an edge → each ticket popped once, each stack entry pushed and popped once → O(E) after the O(E log E) sort for lexical order, vs exponential worst case for backtracking
elevated: Sorting destinations in reverse and popping from the end of each list → the smallest destination is always taken first in O(1) → lexical order at no extra per-step cost
reference: Fleury's algorithm and its O(E²) bridge test

compress.prompt: Without looking, trace the dead-end case [["JFK","KUL"],["JFK","NRT"],["NRT","JFK"]] with a stack and a route list, then write two sentences on why reversing the route gives a valid itinerary.
checklist: JFK → KUL, stuck: KUL goes on the route first
back at JFK, take NRT → JFK, then all stuck: pop the rest
route KUL, JFK, NRT, JFK reversed: JFK, NRT, JFK, KUL
the stuck node is the end (the +1-in node); later detours come before it
each ticket is used once, never undone

retrieve.q: Explain why a node other than the end can't be where the walk first gets stuck, in a graph that has an Eulerian path.
answer: every time you enter a balanced node you used one of its in-edges
it has as many out-edges as in-edges, so an unused out-edge remains
only the node with an extra in-edge can run out first

retrieve.q: Trace the card's 5-ticket example: which ticket is taken at each step, and when does the first pop to the route happen?
answer: JFK → ATL (smaller than SFO), ATL → JFK, JFK → SFO, SFO → ATL, ATL → SFO
after 5 pushes every ticket is used; SFO is stuck and is written first
then 5 more pops; reversed: JFK, ATL, JFK, SFO, ATL, SFO

retrieve.q: Greedy smallest-first, backtracking DFS, Fleury, Hierholzer: which of them are correct, and what does each cost for 10⁴ tickets?
answer: greedy: fast but wrong on dead ends
Fleury: correct, but a bridge test per step, O(E²) ≈ 10⁸

compare.q: Backtracking also solves Reconstruct Itinerary. What does it do at a dead end that Hierholzer doesn't, and why is Hierholzer allowed to skip it?
answer: backtracking undoes the last tickets and tries another order
Hierholzer keeps the dead end and writes it as the path's end
the degree argument guarantees the dead end is the end node, so nothing needs undoing

compare.q: Both use an explicit stack and pop when stuck. What does each write down, and when?
answer: flood fill marks a cell when it is pushed (pre-order)
Hierholzer writes a node when it has no unused edge left (post-order)
post-order + reverse is what orders the path correctly, like finishing order in topological sort

predict.q: Add the ticket SFO → JFK to the card's five. Predict the degree picture, whether this is a path or a circuit, and the new itinerary.
predict.answer: Every airport becomes balanced (JFK 2 out, 2 in; ATL 2/2; SFO 2/2), so it's an Euler circuit that must start and end at JFK. The itinerary is JFK, ATL, JFK, SFO, ATL, SFO, JFK: the same walk as before, extended by the new ticket back home.

apply.task: Check the degrees and then run the stack by hand on [["JFK","A"],["A","B"],["B","A"],["JFK","C"],["C","JFK"]]. Show where smallest-first greedy gets stuck, and the itinerary Hierholzer returns.
apply.done: Degrees: JFK +1, A −1, B and C balanced. Greedy goes JFK → A → B → A and strands C's tickets; Hierholzer writes A, B, A first and returns JFK, C, JFK, A, B, A.
apply.hint: The dead end is A, the −1 node, so it must be last.
